questions.question: Present the four arguments for deliberate industrial development, and balance them with the infant-industry caution.
questions.expected_answer: One: value added — each processing stage multiplies the worth of the raw material (chrome ore to ferrochrome to stainless steel to finished goods), and the country performing a stage keeps its wages, profits and taxes; processing at home before export is beneficiation — export the product, not the ore. Two: employment — manufacturing absorbs semi-skilled labour at a scale mechanised mining cannot and high-skill services will not, making factories the classic ladder for an economy with mass unemployment. Three: stability — a commodity exporter rides world price swings, flush in booms and gutted in slumps, while a diversified industrial base spreads income across many products and markets. Four: linkages — a factory pulls suppliers into existence behind it (backward linkages: components, toolrooms, transport) and users and sellers in front of it (forward linkages: dealers, mechanics, finance), so one plant anchors hundreds of firms and manufacturing acts as a growth engine. The caution: support is never free — protection taxes consumers through higher prices, subsidies consume public money, and support without a finish line breeds industries that stay comfortable rather than becoming competitive, so every strategy must eventually show its industry can stand in world markets.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's main industrial and regional development instruments by name, including the SEZ package and one corridor, and state the lesson of apartheid decentralisation.
questions.expected_answer: Industrial: the National Industrial Policy Framework of 2007, implemented through rolling Industrial Policy Action Plans that target priority sectors; the Automotive Production and Development Programme, rewarding local production and investment through import-duty credits and allowances — the reason seven global carmakers assemble here; the Clothing and Textiles Competitiveness Programme; Section 12I tax allowances for large industrial investments; the Black Industrialists Scheme; patient finance through the Industrial Development Corporation; and localisation — designated public procurement obliging state entities to buy buses, rail stock, cables and uniforms locally — under the National Development Plan's goal of raising manufacturing's share. Regional: spatial development initiatives concentrating investment along corridors with real potential — flagship the Maputo Development Corridor, the N4 toll road and rail and border upgrades linking Gauteng to Maputo's closer port through public-private partnership; and special economic zones under the SEZ Act of 2014 — serviced precincts tied to ports or airports offering 15 percent corporate tax, building allowances, employment tax incentives and duty-free inputs for export production, with named zones at Coega (largest, with the deep-water port of Ngqura), East London (vehicle assembly), Richards Bay (minerals and metals), Dube TradePort (perishables and electronics beside King Shaka), Saldanha Bay (oil and gas) and Tshwane (automotive). The decentralisation lesson: apartheid paid factories to relocate to homeland border areas, and they died when the subsidies stopped — location incentives without genuine economic foundations buy temporary factories, not development.

questions.question: Evaluate whether South Africa's industrial and regional strategies are appropriate, using the four benchmarks from the lesson and ending with a defensible one-sentence verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Benchmark one, best practice: successful industrialisers tied support to export performance, kept it temporary, and invested heavily in skills and infrastructure; the APDP passes the export test and rates highest, while open-ended protection of uncompetitive sectors rates lowest. Benchmark two, results: manufacturing's share of GDP has slid over two decades from above 19 percent toward 12 to 13 percent — deindustrialisation, the most damning aggregate fact; the zones are uneven, with Coega and Dube TradePort holding real tenants, jobs and exports while several others remain serviced land without occupants; vehicle assembly thrives while clothing employment collapsed despite support — a balanced verdict names both columns. Benchmark three, binding constraints: no incentive outweighs failing electricity, congested ports, unreliable rail and scarce skills, so sequencing matters — repairing the network industries may do more than any new subsidy; this is the strongest single evaluation point. Benchmark four, cost and governance: measure rands per sustainable job, treat any zone needing permanent subsidy as the homeland mistake rebranded, and remember that policy certainty and clean procurement are location factors investors price like freight. Verdict: the direction is defensible and the flagship programmes deliver, but the strategy underachieves while the foundations crumble — fix the constraints and the incentives can finally bite.
